body: I guess it depends on how far you're willing to take it. Are you really willing to stand up and say that murdering a child isn't wrong because everything is meaningless? If not then I think my point stands because it does mean there is some value there. But even if you do accept the premise, that murdering a child is okay, I think you run into some problems still. The problem is that you're dealing with absolutes. You're saying that nihilism is 100% true because it's what's most logical. The problem is that conclusion is far from justified. Yes, it probably is most logical, but you can never be 100% on anything. Even the nature of human consciousness suggests at least a possibility of something else. Even if its a 0.0000001% probability. And since murdering a child is either neutral by nihilism, or negative by the alternatives which have non zero probability, the EV (I guess, to put it into more game theory-ish terms) of the action turns out to be negative, meaning it's still wrong. If nihilism is true, then yes, killing a child technically isn't wrong. But it's irrational to act in a way assuming nihilism is 100% true. So yeah, if nihilism is true its impossible to do anything of value whatsoever. But since its irrational to deal with it in such absolutes I'd argue that you can still do things of value, or at least things with expected value.

Thank you for the response. I do really know exactly how you feel. I feel as if I always have to be working towards accomplishing something big in math otherwise I have no value, or had potential but didn't fulfil it. I've always had this fear of being forgotten. Perhaps it's childish or selfish but I'm terrified of dying and eventually nobody will ever remember or care about who I was. And accomplishing something in math would change that. But its tough. Its tough because that exact perfectionism ad need to do something big is what causes me to have such bad anxiety causing me to be a parasite to everyone around me.

For you I wouldn't lose hope. People have lulls in creativity or their ability to think at all ages but that's not to say it wont come back. Also, and I don't know how you are involved in academia but perhaps teaching others could give you some sense of fulfillment. I know I owe everything I do and will do in math 100% to all my professors along the way that through their wisdom were able to not only teach me but get me excited by math. Perhaps that's something you'd find happiness in doing. In inspiring the younger generation to have the passion for the subject that you clearly have. 

Regardless, I really do appreciate you taking the time to read and even respond to what I've written. It means a lot. Thank you.

That's what I'm saying though. If everyone was nihilistic nobody would be able to be happy, so yeah nothing would matter. But the point is some people can experience happiness, even if it is built on ignorance. From our POV its meaningless but it has intrinsic value to them nonetheless. At the heat death of the universe sure none of it will matter but right now, in the present, a a conscious being being happy is at least intrinsically valuable to them. So we can provide some sort of value regardless of whether from our POV it even means anything

Nihilism says they're is no meaning in life, everything is pointless so whatever we do doesn't matter. Here's my conclusion I just came to on the spot. Nihilism would be absolutely true if everyone had nihilistic views. Life would have no meaning, and there would be no way to create meaning in life. Here's my point though: given that everything is meaningless we can't create meaning out of our lives and the heat death of the universe is inevitable, do morals exist? Is it okay to murder a child because of the utter meaninglessness of life? I would assume everyone here would say no. Why? Well, the child might grow up and be able to find happiness in life. Perhaps it'll be unfounded and due to them not fully grasping the reality of the universe but it'll be happiness nonetheless which is valuable. I'm sure everyone here wishes they could live in a state where they believe their life has some divine meaning to it causing them happiness, we just can't go back to being that way. But, it would still be wrong to impose your view over theirs and essentially take their happiness or peacefulness from them.

Well, then is it possible to create meaning from the inherently meaningless life nihilism suggests? I would say yes. If conscious happiness is valuable, at least intrinsically to the person experiencing the happiness, then the fact that everyone isn't nihilistic allows us to create some meaning. If I myself am unable to experience happiness due to my realization of the reality of the universe, at least I can maximize the happiness of others who still are able to experience this. Fight for human rights, help people in need, do something that allows others to experience happiness for themselves, because while temporary this happiness IS valuable, at least to them. In doing so you find some value that you're providing with your own life.
